After 70, a few of the most common pills in American medicine cabinets are linked with memory trouble, and most of them look completely harmless. Researchers at the University of Washington in Seattle followed nearly 3,500 adults over 65 for about seven years. The ones who'd taken the most of one family of these pills, more than three years' worth of daily doses, had a 54 percent higher risk of dementia. People who took them only now and then had no higher risk at all.

This video counts down six everyday pills: the PM on the box, the allergy pill from the old days, the pill for dizzy spells, the antidepressant you didn't know you were taking, the pill that calms your nerves or puts you to sleep, and number one, a pill people take for a problem nowhere near the brain.

After 65, a daily hot shower strips the oil film that keeps bacteria out of your skin. Cracked shins are where cellulitis begins. That tight, flaky feeling on your lower legs ten minutes after the towel is not "dry skin you've always had" — it is the barrier dissolving faster than it rebuilds, and the gap it leaves is the same one that sends older adults to the emergency room with a swollen, brick-red leg.

Sleeping under 6 or over 9 hours after 60 tracks with dementia years later — and the long night is the risk nobody questions. The safe window sits near seven hours, and most people past 60 have never once measured theirs honestly. This video gives you the number, the reason your brain depends on it, and what to do when your bladder, your hip, or your racing mind will not let you reach it.
